old: and Hurrian groups in the northern hills
new: and probably early Hurrian groups (first named in texts only after c. 2300 BCE) in the northern hills
source: Hurrians first documented at Urkesh in the later 3rd millennium, allied with Akkad by Naram-Sin's reign; earlier presence only inferred: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurrians

old: Mentuhotep II reunites Egypt, beginning the Middle Kingdom (c. 2055 BCE)
new: Mentuhotep II, king from c. 2055 BCE, reunites Egypt, beginning the Middle Kingdom (c. 2040 BCE)
source: CAH 3rd ed. vol. I pt 2 (1971), ch. XX (Hayes), p. 479: accession 2060, Heracleopolis falls "about 2040 B.C."; Shaw, Oxford History of Ancient Egypt dates accession 2055; Grajetzki via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentuhotep_II (unification shortly before year 39)

old: King David rules a new kingdom of Israel from Jerusalem
new: King David, according to the Bible, rules a new kingdom of Israel from Jerusalem
source: Extent and nature of the united monarchy has no scholarly consensus (Finkelstein low chronology vs. Mazar, Dever, Faust): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Israel_(united_monarchy)

old: the Phoenicians of Tyre and Sidon are spreading their alphabet across the Mediterranean
new: the Phoenicians of Tyre and Sidon have developed the alphabet their traders will later carry across the Mediterranean
source: Oldest Phoenician inscriptions 10th c. BCE; adaptations (Greek, Old Italic, Anatolian) begin from the 9th c., Greek alphabet 8th c.: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet ; Phoenician westward colonies 9th c. on (Kition, Carthage 814)

old: under him and his son Solomon it will become a regional power
new: the Bible says that under him and his son Solomon it became a regional power, though archaeologists debate how large their kingdom really was
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Israel_(united_monarchy) ("no current consensus"; Solomon's 10th-c. reign "uncertain"); CAH III.1 (1982) still follows the biblical maximal view, now disputed

old: The hill country of Canaan, from the Negev toward Damascus
new: The hill country of Canaan; the Bible's larger realm, from the Negev toward Damascus, is debated
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Israel_(united_monarchy)

old: the kingdom of the legendary King Midas
new: the kingdom of King Midas, famous from Greek legend but a real ruler (the Mita of Assyrian records)
source: Cambridge Ancient History, 2nd ed., vol. III part 2 (1991), ch. 34 (Mellink), p. 622-3: Midas = "Mita of Mushki" in Assyrian records; also pp. 91-2 (Sargon II's wars with Mita)

old: Sennacherib of Assyria rules an empire from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean, having destroyed the kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE and forced Judah under Hezekiah to pay tribute.
new: Sennacherib of Assyria rules an empire from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean; Assyria destroyed the kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE, and Sennacherib has forced Judah under Hezekiah to pay tribute.
source: Cambridge Ancient History, 2nd ed., vol. III part 2 (1991), ch. 22 (Grayson), pp. 85-6: Samaria captured by Shalmaneser V (726-722), not Sennacherib (705-681); sentence wrongly made Sennacherib the conqueror of Israel

old: and the Medes are uniting in western Iran
new: and the Medes, still divided among many local chiefs, live in western Iran
source: Cambridge Ancient History, 2nd ed., vol. III part 2 (1991), pp. 93-4 (Sargon II takes tribute from "twenty-eight rulers of the land of the Medes") and pp. 129-30 (Median city-rulers under Esarhaddon); Assyrian sources never mention a unified Median state before Cyaxares (615 BCE): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_kingdom

old: Under Thutmose III, from Nubia's Fourth Cataract to the Euphrates
new: Under Thutmose III, from Nubia's Fourth Cataract to the Euphrates; c. 1.0M km² c. 1450 BCE (Taagepera 1978)
source: Taagepera 1978 "Growth-Decline Curves, 3000 to 600 B.C.", as tabulated at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires

old: native independence ended when Cleopatra VII died
new: its independence ended when Cleopatra VII died
source: The profile itself calls the Ptolemies Greek; the last native ruler was Nectanebo II (358-c. 340 BCE, Persian reconquest 342 BCE), so 30 BCE ended Egyptian independence, not native rule: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nectanebo_II
Peak given as Ur III "under Shulgi" (c. 2094-2047 BCE); 2100 BCE precedes his accession. Shulgi dates as in the profile's own ruler list

old: ruling Mesopotamia and parts of western Iran
new: ruling Mesopotamia and parts of western Iran; Taagepera (1978) puts the Neo-Sumerian state at only c. 0.1M km², so 250,000 km² assumes the tributary periphery
source: Taagepera 1978 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires ("Neo-Sumerian Empire" 0.1 Mm², 2000 BC)
Taagepera 1978: Akkadian Empire 0.8 Mm² at 2250 BC, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires

old: Under Naram-Sin, from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean and the Anatolian foothills
new: Under Naram-Sin, from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean and the Anatolian foothills; c. 0.8M km² (Taagepera 1978), though directly ruled land was smaller
source: Taagepera 1978 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires; map border data (clio) gives c. 527,000 km² for 2250-2201 BCE

old: In 626 BCE the Chaldean Nabopolassar threw off Assyrian rule
new: In 626 BCE Nabopolassar, traditionally called a Chaldean, threw off Assyrian rule
source: His origin is unclear; Beaulieu (1998) and Jursa (2007) link his family to Uruk officials; he called himself "son of a nobody": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabopolassar

old: Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II, from the Gulf to the borders of Egypt
new: Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II, from the Gulf to the borders of Egypt; c. 0.5M km² (Taagepera 1978)
source: Taagepera 1978 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires

old: whose merchants ran caravans into Anatolia by 2000 BCE
new: whose merchants ran caravans into Anatolia soon after 2000 BCE
source: Old Assyrian karum at Kanesh, level II c. 1974-1836 BCE (Veenhof, middle chronology): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%BCltepe

old: Under Esarhaddon, from Egypt to western Iran
new: Under Esarhaddon, from Egypt to western Iran; c. 1.4M km² c. 670 BCE (Taagepera 1978)
source: Taagepera 1978; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires
Taagepera 1978: New Hittite Kingdom 0.45 Mm² at 1250-1220 BC, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires

old: Under Suppiluliuma I and his successors, from central Anatolia to Syria
new: Under Suppiluliuma I and his successors, from central Anatolia to Syria; c. 0.45M km² c. 1250-1220 BCE (Taagepera 1978)
source: Taagepera 1978 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires

old: known before only from brief Bible mentions
new: known before only from brief mentions in the Bible and in Egyptian records
source: Before the 1906 Hattusa archive, the Hittites were known from the Bible and from Egyptian sources (the "Kheta" of the Kadesh inscriptions and the Amarna letters): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hittites

Revised order (Shebitku before Shabaka; Tang-i Var inscription of 706 BCE): Shabaka 705-690, Payraudeau 2014, matching the profile's Piye dates 744-714 from the same scheme: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabaka ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piye . Older order: Shabako 716-702, Cambridge Ancient History, 2nd ed., vol. III part 2 (1991), pp. 353 and 689. "714-700" matches neither

old: Made peace with Athens
new: Said to have made peace with Athens (the disputed Peace of Callias)
source: Historicity of the Peace of Callias (c. 449 BCE) is contested (Thucydides silent, Theopompus called it a fabrication): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Callias

old: Under Darius I, from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus
new: Under Darius I, from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus; c. 5.5M km² c. 500 BCE (Taagepera 1979)
source: Taagepera 1979; Turchin, Adams & Hall 2006, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires
